The Bond Market’s Surprising Take on the AI Trade
 
Plus, stocks pop as Anthropic sets a high IPO price
 

Good morning, I’m filling in for Spencer Jakab. The AI trade appears to be back on Thursday as markets get ready to celebrate the Anthropic debut. The AI model developer sold more shares than it planned at a higher price than expected in its initial public offering late Wednesday. At $83 a share it raised $81 billion in the largest-ever IPO. Stocks were buoyed by the news, with Nasdaq futures up 2% in premarket trading.

A clearer sky

 

Judging by stocks lately, you might think that basically everything that can go wrong in the AI trade has gone wrong.

 

Bonds are sending a different signal.

 

Over the past week or so, the bond market—reputed to obsess about what can go wrong—seemed to get a little more comfortable with AI-related risks.

 

Bonds issued by “hyperscaler” AI computing giants such as Alphabet, Amazon and Meta Platforms actually outperformed. Last week, the difference between yields on their debt versus Treasurys narrowed more than spreads for other corporate bonds, according to the JPMorgan U.S. Liquid Index tracking investment-grade issues. This means investors were demanding less extra return to compensate for the risks of holding that debt.

 

Likewise, across more than two dozen bonds issued to finance the build-out of data centers for AI computing, the average spread has narrowed since Nov. 9, according to a Journal analysis of MarketAxess data. That move has been led by data-center bonds with high-yield “junk” ratings.

 

AI-related bonds still often trade at relatively higher yields than similar corporate bonds, both in the high-grade and junk markets. So investors are hardly sanguine.

 

Yet the logic of the past week or two appears to be that if future data-center construction is becoming dicier, data centers that do get built can become more valuable. And if AI companies have to focus more on maximizing today’s revenues, that could favor bonds over stocks, which are priced for future growth.

 

Bonds may also take heart from Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings Tuesday, which showed the company has kept up its strong performance.

 

But here’s the rub: Many investors won’t have full exposure to the AI bond market.

 

A lot of passive-index investors may be effectively underweight data-center financing bonds. Many of those bonds are a specific class of securities that are privately placed to qualified investors. Such bonds also currently don’t qualify for inclusion in the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index. This is the basis for some of the largest passive bond funds.

 

Active funds can buy these bonds, and other passive benchmarks can include them. Still, they are often underrepresented in the kinds of funds many everyday investors buy.

 

Among the disclosed holdings of investment-grade data-center bonds, only 3% are in ETFs, according to a recent tally from JPMorgan Chase credit strategists led by Nathaniel Rosenbaum. By contrast, ETFs represent 17% of those holdings for highly rated hyperscalers’ debt.

 

As of October, mutual funds and ETFs were often underweight junk-rated data-center bonds relative to their weight in benchmarks, according to Bloomberg data compiled by Goldman Sachs credit strategists.

 

Investors are used to getting more than their fill of AI exposure in the stock market. In the bond market, it’s the opposite situation.

 

Some investors might be all right with that, given the many fears swirling around the AI build-out. But those who want the full benefit of diversification will have to seek it out.
